newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians asks world to stop Israeli settlement.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians asks world to stop Israeli settlement.

text.p: Palestinians praying on Friday beside the Arab East Jerusalem hilltop where Israel plans a new Jewish settlement appealed to the world to block the project they said threatened the Middle East peace process.
"All leaders of the world: We appeal to you from this besieged village to work to cancel the decision...to build on our land," a Moslem cleric leading prayers said.

The pine-covered Jabal Abu Ghneim, known by Israelis as Har Homa, is located next to the Arab village of Um Tuba. Residents said Israel confiscated their portion of the mountain in 1991 to build 6,500 homes for Jews.

Israeli troops and police armed with automatic weapons surrounded a soccer field at the foot of the hill while some 500 Palestinian men, women and children prayed. An Israeli plane circled overhead during the protest.
Tensions rose briefly when some 30 Palestinian youths tried to ascend the hill, where paramilitary Israeli border police were stationed. The incident ended without violence.

"I think that the bulldozer of the peace process is stronger than the bulldozers of Netanyahu," said Abbas Zaki, a Palestinian lawmaker and a leader in the mainstream PLO Fatah faction, urging young Arabs to avoid clashing with the Israelis.
But Zaki said Palestinian patience could run out when work does begin to build the settlement.
"We as a leadership, we haven't any idea to fight. We have ideas for building and peace. But our people have enough courage to deal with the aggression," he said in English.
Worshippers dispersed without incident after the prayers.

About 17,000 Palestinians attended prayers at al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem's Old City, Islam's third holiest site, Israel Radio said. Israel had deployed large numbers of policemen in the Old city. But prayers ended peacefully.
Wednesday's decision by the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to build on Jabal Abu Ghneim has sparked criticism worldwide.

Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and views all of the city as its capital, a view unrecognised by the international community. Palestinians want East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday attacked the decision to build as a breach of peace agreements. But he heeded U.S. warnings to keep the lid on violent protests.
Palestinian and Israeli analysts believe Arafat will not openly call for confrontation, particularly ahead of his scheduled meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton next week.
Arafat cannot let Israeli settlement go unchallenged but neither he nor Netanyahu has an interest in a replay of last September's violence sparked by Israeli action in East Jerusalem, analysts say.
Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died in gun battles after Netanyahu opened a tourist tunnel near Islamic holy shrines in Jerusalem.
Netanyahu was grilled by right-wing ministers at the weekly cabinet meeting over reports he had made a quid pro quo agreement with Arafat over the decision to build.

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz said on Thursday Netanyahu had an unwritten agreement with Arafat that Israel would increase the size of its next pullout from the West Bank in exchange for a promise to contain Palestinian reaction to the Har Homa plan.
A communique issued after the meeting said:

"The prime minister again emphasised that there is not yet any conclusion on the scope of the first stage of the further redeploment and that there is no truth to reports that there has already been a deal on this matter."

The U.N. Security Council was to hold informal consultations on Friday on a request it meet on Israel's building plans. The Arab League said it would hold an emergency meeting of its permanent representatives on the plan on Sunday.
